\section[stressado]{stressado — stressed}

\label{lesson:PT-C361-stressado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the rise, then the Portuguese for the qualification.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: stressado}
\textbf{stressado} — \textquotedblleft{}stressed\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ando muito stressado com os exames.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I have been very stressed about the exams.}
\end{quote}

European spelling; in Brazil \emph{estressado}. A woman says \emph{stressada}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{stressado} is built on \emph{stress}, borrowed from English \emph{stress}, which EtymDB traces to Middle English \emph{destresse} \textquotedblleft{}distress\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); that word is usually traced through Old French to Latin \emph{strictus}, the participle of \emph{stringere} \textquotedblleft{}to draw tight\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{stressado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{stressado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{stressado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the rise, then the Portuguese for the qualification, then say \emph{stressado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does stressado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Stressed\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[esgotado]{esgotado — worn out, exhausted; sold out}

\label{lesson:PT-C361-esgotado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the qualification, then the Portuguese for stressed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: esgotado}
\textbf{esgotado} — \textquotedblleft{}worn out, exhausted; sold out\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Depois de doze horas de trabalho, estou esgotado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{After twelve hours of work, I am worn out.}
\end{quote}

Also sold out: \emph{os bilhetes estão esgotados}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{esgotado} is the participle of \emph{esgotar} \textquotedblleft{}to drain to the last drop\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{es-} and \emph{gota} \textquotedblleft{}drop\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{gutta} \textquotedblleft{}a drop of a fluid\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{esgotado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{esgotado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the qualification, then the Portuguese for stressed, then say \emph{esgotado} again

\section[as horas extraordinárias]{as horas extraordinárias — the overtime}

\label{lesson:PT-C361-horas-extraordinarias}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for stressed, then the Portuguese for worn out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: as horas extraordinárias}
\textbf{as horas extraordinárias} — \textquotedblleft{}the overtime\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fiz muitas horas extraordinárias este mês.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I did a lot of overtime this month.}
\end{quote}

In speech \emph{as horas extra}; in Brazil \emph{as horas extras}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{hora} is inherited from Latin \emph{hōra} \textquotedblleft{}hour\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{extraordinário} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{extraordinārius} \textquotedblleft{}out of the common order\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), on \emph{ōrdō} \textquotedblleft{}order\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[eficiente]{eficiente — efficient}

\label{lesson:PT-C361-eficiente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for worn out, then the Portuguese for the overtime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: eficiente}
\textbf{eficiente} — \textquotedblleft{}efficient\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A nova máquina é mais eficiente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The new machine is more efficient.}
\end{quote}

\emph{A eficiência} — efficiency.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{eficiente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{efficiēns} (EtymDB), the present participle of \emph{efficere} \textquotedblleft{}to bring about\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[a produtividade]{a produtividade — the productivity}

\label{lesson:PT-C361-produtividade}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the overtime, then the Portuguese for efficient.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a produtividade}
\textbf{a produtividade} — \textquotedblleft{}the productivity\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A produtividade sobe quando as pessoas descansam.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Productivity goes up when people rest.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Produtivo} — productive.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{produtividade} is built on \emph{produtivo} \textquotedblleft{}productive\textquotedblright{}, from Late Latin \emph{prōductīvus}, on \emph{prōdūcere} \textquotedblleft{}to lead forth\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{dūcere} \textquotedblleft{}to lead\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
